title: Thinking Machines ships Inkling 2 Mini — open-weights looped MoE that fits on a laptop
subtitle: The Mira Murati–led lab released the 26B-parameter mixture-of-experts model on Hugging Face under Apache 2.0, pitched as the first frontier-grade open-weights model that runs locally.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Thinking Machines, the Mira Murati lab that spun up in 2024, released Inkling 2 Mini on Thursday as open weights on Hugging Face under Apache 2.0. The model is a 'looped' mixture-of-experts transformer of roughly 26.4 billion total parameters and about 20 GB of weights on disk. The company is also hosting it on its Tinker platform for inference and fine-tuning. The pitch is that it is the first model in its capability tier to run comfortably on a developer laptop; Futurum's writeup places it ahead of sub-100B open-weights competitors on agentic coding benchmarks, though that comparison is third-party.

The 'looped' architecture is the interesting part. Inkling 2 recycles a shared block of parameters through multiple passes at inference, a form of weight tying that lets the model present a larger effective compute budget than its memory footprint suggests. It is the same architectural idea behind the original Inkling 2 Small from earlier this month, scaled down for local deployment. Open weights plus a permissive license means third-party quantizations will land within days, which is the real distribution channel for models of this size.

The release lands in a crowded open-weights week. Alibaba's Qwen line, Moonshot's Kimi K3, Meta's Muse Spark and Mistral Large 4 all compete for the top of the leaderboards. What Thinking Machines is betting on is a narrower claim: that frontier capability on consumer hardware, under a license corporate customers can actually accept, is a different product than the same capability behind an API. If that bet is right, Inkling 2 Mini is the start of a line, not a one-off. The company has disclosed it is also working on an Inkling 2 Flash for latency-sensitive inference.

A note for learners: the useful question about any open-weights release is not 'how does it rank?' but 'what does the license let you do?' Apache 2.0 is permissive enough for commercial deployment, modification and redistribution — meaning teams can fine-tune on proprietary data, host internally, and not pay per token. That economic shape is why open-weights models have become infrastructure for enterprise AI even when they trail closed models on headline benchmarks. The weights are the asset; the benchmark is marketing.
